HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) does not address conflicting or superseded information at all: it simply indexes every passage into an OpenIE knowledge graph with synonym edges and retrieves via Personalized PageRank, with no mechanism for deleting or overriding stale states [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s7.p4]. Its only online filtering is an LLM relevance filter over retrieved triples, which selects relevant seeds but does not resolve contradictions [2502.14802#s10.p1]. New information is thus accumulated rather than reconciled, and the papers' stated limitations concern NER/OpenIE errors and scalability, not conflict handling [2405.14831#s21.p2].

GC-Mem, by contrast, is built specifically for state mutation: it formalizes Semantic Shadowing, where an updated entity state leaves the old state in memory and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale, semantically equivalent but contradictory chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. It applies an inference-time temporal dominance operator Φ_T with a pairwise NLI contradiction detector over the retrieved candidate set, excising any chunk contradicted by a newer one, so that if one valid chunk is retrieved all older contradictory chunks are removed [2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. This avoids heuristic time-decay and multi-factor scoring, which the paper shows can protect entrenched errors [2609.16073#s1.p1][2609.16073#s17.p3]. Its effectiveness is bounded by detector recall (>50% required; gpt-4o's 36.6% recall yields only +4.0 pp) [2609.16073#s16.p3][2609.16073#s20.p1], and it adds O(k²) checking cost (~250 ms) [2609.16073#s20.p2].

respuesta: HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) has no explicit mechanism for handling new or conflicting information: it is an offline-indexed, append-only graph index (OpenIE triples + passage nodes, retrieved via Personalized PageRank) [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2405.14831#s5.p2]. It never overwrites or supersedes facts; when contradictory facts coexist in context, it simply retrieves both, and on FactConsolidation it reaches only 54.0 single-hop and 5.0 multi-hop accuracy [2507.05257#s21.p3]. GC-Mem instead keeps the store append-only but excises contradicted older chunks from the retrieved context via temporal dominance [2609.16073#s9.p4], reaching 97.3% conflict-resolution accuracy versus 56.8% for standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3]. So the difference is at retrieval time: HippoRAG surfaces all versions, while GC-Mem filters out the stale ones.

The paper is A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents (arXiv 2502.12110). It organizes an agent's memory as atomic notes in an interconnected network following the Zettelkasten method, a note-taking method attributed to German sociologist Niklas Luhmann [2502.12110#s6.p1]. Each note carries LLM-generated keywords, tags, and context plus an embedding, and when a new note is added the top-k similar notes are retrieved and the LLM decides which links to create [2502.12110#s8.p2][2502.12110#s8.p6].

A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents (arXiv 2502.12110) links an agent's notes to each other following the Zettelkasten method, the note-taking system of German sociologist Niklas Luhmann [2502.12110#s6.p1]. Each note stores a set of linked memories, and when a new note is added, cosine similarity selects top-k candidates and the LLM decides which links to create [2502.12110#s8.p2][2502.12110#s8.p6].

They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. WikiLoop explicitly trains its knowledge-base construction on downstream feedback: a Builder edits an agent-native Wiki and is rewarded by the change in downstream navigation utility, measured as a paired before/after difference under a frozen Navigator, with a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s7.p17]. HippoRAG 2, by contrast, builds its graph index offline with an LLM (OpenIE triples, synonym edges, passage nodes) and uses an LLM triple filter at query time, but its components are used off-the-shelf without fine-tuning and no downstream-answer reward is used to improve the knowledge base [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s10.p1]; its predecessor HippoRAG likewise uses all components off-the-shelf without fine-tuning [2405.14831#s21.p2]. So WikiLoop closes the loop between construction and downstream use, whereas HippoRAG 2 optimizes construction and retrieval without downstream feedback.

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG 2 downstream feedback knowledge graph improvement

respuesta: They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph (OpenIE triples, synonym edges, passage nodes) offline and retrieves with query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank; its construction is not trained or corrected by downstream answer feedback — the LLM filter operates online at query time, and the paper reports no feedback-driven improvement of the graph itself [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. WikiLoop instead explicitly couples construction to downstream use: a Builder applies schema-constrained patches to the Wiki and is rewarded by the change in downstream navigation utility, measured as a paired before/after difference under a frozen Navigator, minus a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p9][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s7.p17]. This guarded marginal-utility credit is trained with GRPO/GSPO, and the guard term cuts Guard Regression from 0.046 to 0.016 while affected ΔAC stays near 12 [2607.26604#s8.p11][2607.26604#s12.p12]. In short, HippoRAG 2's structure is fixed at indexing time and only filtered at retrieval, whereas WikiLoop learns its structured KB from downstream feedback [2607.26604#s1.p1].
